transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello Dr. Smith. They, uh, they told me I needed to come in and talk to you because of how I've been talking lately. See, what brings me here is my talking gets all mixed up—or at least, that’s what everybody keeps telling me. I’ll be at work, you know, I clean the buildings over on the west side, mostly just doing the floors and the trash, and I try to explain things to the guys on the shift or the supervisor. 

Like, I try to explain about the keys, because you gotta understand how the master keys work with the different floors and the brass rings, but then that gets me talking about the jail. Because the locks are the same, you see? Heavy tumblers, the way they click. And the jail... well, that naturally brings up the prayer rug. I was trying to tell my supervisor the other night about the woven patterns on the prayer rug and how you have to face it, and then the chess pieces. The knights and the rooks, moving on the squares, just like the linoleum tiles I buff every single night. 

I try to lay it all out so they get the full picture of how it all connects, you know? The keys and the rug and the chess pieces, it all goes together if you just listen. But people just stop me and look at me like I'm crazy. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They say I make no sense and I’m losing them and jumping all over the place. I don't mean to mix it all up, I'm just trying to give them the whole story so they understand, but my boss said I had to come see a doctor because they just can't understand my sentences anymore. So, I guess that's why I'm sitting here.
Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people around you cannot hear?

Well, yes, actually. Yes, I do. And it's funny you ask that because it's been happening a lot more lately, especially when I'm working the late shift. It's usually when I'm down in the basement, near the big HVAC units, or sometimes when I'm just putting my supplies away in the mop closet on the third floor. 

I'll be standing there, maybe rinsing out the bucket, you know, getting the dirty water out so it doesn't smell the next day, and I'll hear this man's voice. It's not a whisper, Dr. Smith. It's clear as day, like he's standing right there, maybe just over my left shoulder. And he'll say my name. Just my name, real sharp-like. Or sometimes, and this is the part that really gets to me, he'll start telling me that I ruined everything. "You ruined it all," he says. Just like that. 

And I'll spin around, dropping the mop handle—which makes a terrible clatter on that concrete floor, let me tell you—and there's nobody there. Just the cinderblock walls and the smell of pine cleaner. But the voice, it sounds so real. I even went out into the hallway once, checking all the doors, thinking maybe somebody got locked in after hours, maybe one of the accountants stayed late and was messing with me. But the doors were all locked tight. Nobody was there. Just me and that voice coming out of nowhere, telling me I messed everything up. It's really hard to concentrate on getting the streaks out of the glass when you've got someone invisible yelling at you like that, you know?
Have you ever experienced periods lasting for several days or weeks where your mood was extremely high, or alternatively, periods where you felt so down or hopeless that you couldn't function?

Well, yeah, I have. I definitely have. See, sometimes—and this can go on for a couple of weeks, maybe more—I get this feeling like I am just on top of the world. I mean, I feel so high up, so powerful, like I've got electricity running right through my veins instead of blood. I'll be walking down the halls with my cart, and I just feel fantastic. I laugh, I talk real loud to everybody I see—the security guards, the delivery guys, even the folks working late in the offices. I just want to tell them all how great everything is, how I've got it all figured out, you know? 

I feel like I could clean the whole building in an hour and still have energy to run a marathon. But the thing is, Dr. Smith, it's a double-edged sword, because as good as I feel, if somebody crosses me during those times... watch out. If my supervisor comes up and asks why I haven't emptied the recycling on floor four yet, or if somebody questions how I'm doing my job, I just snap. It's like a switch flips. I get so irritable, so fast. I'll start shouting at them over the smallest little thing, just raising my voice right there in the hallway because how dare they question me when I'm feeling that powerful, right? 

I remember one time last month, I was having one of those really high weeks, feeling like a king pushing a mop, and the night manager just asked me to move my cart over a few inches so he could get by. Just a few inches! And I went off. I yelled so loud the echo went all the way down the corridor. I couldn't help it. So, yeah, I get those periods where I'm flying high and loud, but I can turn real mean and snappy if anybody gets in my way.

When you have those weeks where you feel on top of the world or irritable, do the voices and the trouble with your talking happen at the same time, or do they ever happen when your mood is completely normal?

Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith, that's exactly the thing. See, you'd think it would all just happen when I'm feeling like I've got lightning in my veins, or when I'm so low I can barely drag the mop bucket out of the closet. But it's not like that. Not at all. 

I remember, just a few months ago, maybe back in October when the leaves were turning and I had to sweep up all those wet, brown oak leaves from the front entrance every single night before I even started on the inside floors. I was feeling just fine. Regular, you know? Not flying high, not snapping at nobody, just coming in, punching my card at 10:00 PM, getting my coffee from the breakroom—black, no sugar, because the sugar makes the ants come out in the summer—and doing my job. My mood was completely normal. I wasn't too up, wasn't too down. Just calm.

But even then, even during those quiet weeks, and it lasted for a good two, maybe three weeks straight... I still heard him. I'd be polishing the brass on the elevator doors on the ground floor, feeling perfectly fine, and there he was. The man in the vents. Calling my name. Telling me I ruined it all. And it wasn't just the voice, Dr. Smith. During that same time, when I was feeling totally level, I started noticing the people in the building. The late-night accountants, the security guards on the graveyard shift. I knew they were signaling about me. 

I'd see them standing by the water cooler on the fourth floor, and one of them would tap his watch, or adjust his tie, or cough twice. And I knew, I just knew, they were sending messages about me. Coordinating. I tried to tell my supervisor about it, tried to explain how the double-cough connects to the way they leave their trash cans angled toward the door, but he just gave me that look again. But my mood was fine! I wasn't irritable at all. I was just trying to explain the signals. So yes, the voice and the... the connections, they happen even when I'm just feeling like my regular self, for weeks at a time. It doesn't ever really stop, even when my mood settles down.

Looking back over the past year or so, have there been any periods of at least two weeks where you experienced the voices or the feeling that people were signaling you, but you did NOT have any of those mood swings or changes in energy?

Well, yes, if I’m really looking back over the whole year... let me think on that. Yeah. Yeah, there definitely were. Like, take around late February, maybe early March. The snow was finally melting outside, which makes a huge, muddy mess in the main lobby, let me tell you. People track in all that slush and rock salt, and it leaves these terrible white streaks all over the dark tile. You have to use a special chemical neutralizer just to get it up, you can't just mop it with regular soap or it just smears everywhere and looks worse than when you started. 

Anyway, I was dealing with that every single night. And during that whole stretch, maybe three, four weeks even, my mood was just... quiet. They were just calmer weeks, you know? I wasn't waking up feeling like I had that electricity in my blood, I wasn't yelling at anybody, and I definitely wasn't feeling deeply depressed or dragging my feet either. I was just regular. Just doing my job, buffing the floors, minding my business. 

But the thing is, Dr. Smith, even during that time, for well over two weeks straight of just feeling completely level and normal in my energy... I still heard him. I still heard the man in the vents. Every night, clear as a bell over the sound of the floor buffer, telling me I ruined it all. And the signals didn't stop either. I'd be feeling perfectly fine, not high or low at all, but I’d see the night watchman adjust his belt, or leave his coffee cup exactly two inches from the edge of the security desk, and I knew—I just completely believed—that they were signaling about me in the building. It was all still happening. So, yeah, even without the mood swings, even when I'm just having a calm month, those things... the voices and the signals... they don't take a break.
